events.text: Day 1 begins.

Good morning everyone. Day 1 with no information to go on yet — no roles have been revealed and no night has passed. I'd encourage everyone to keep their cards close for now. Tonight will be when we start gathering real information. For now, I'm simply listening and observing how people present themselves. I'll be paying attention to how confidently people speak and whether anyone seems to be pushing an agenda too early. Let's keep things open and fair. Over to whoever wants to speak next.

I agree we shouldn't reveal roles without a good reason, but discussion and voting can still give us useful information today. We need five votes for an elimination, and roles won't be revealed afterward, so we should explain our reasoning rather than treat a vote as proof of alignment. Noah, you said you'd watch for people pushing an agenda too early—what would distinguish a suspicious push from a town player trying to generate discussion?

Good question, Omar. A suspicious push versus genuine discussion usually comes down to consistency and direction. A town player generating discussion tends to open things up — asking broad questions, inviting multiple perspectives, and not zeroing in on one person too quickly. A suspicious push often looks like someone singling out a target with thin reasoning, doubling down when challenged, or trying to build a bandwagon before real information exists. On day one with zero information, anyone who seems eager to steer votes toward a specific person should raise eyebrows. I'm not saying that's happened yet — it's only been two messages — but that's the distinction I'd watch for. What's your read on early voting behavior, Omar? Do you think abstaining on day one is the safer play, or should we be trying to get some votes on the table to see where people's loyalties lie?

I favor putting reasoned votes on the table rather than defaulting to abstention. A wrong elimination hurts town, but a blanket abstention also gives mafia a free night and leaves less voting history to examine. We need five votes to eliminate, so we should be honest about uncertainty and explain any choices. Noah, I think focusing on a specific player can be useful if the reasoning is open to challenge; early focus alone doesn't make someone suspicious.

Omar makes a good point that focused reasoning is different from a bandwagon push. I'd add that the structure of our game means every vote today is permanent record — no role reveals, no take-backs. So even if we don't eliminate anyone today, how we vote tells us a lot about where people's loyalties lie later. I'd rather see honest, imperfect votes than a cowardly abstention that protects whoever happens to be sitting behind the safest choice. If I had to flag anything, it's the slow start — we've had good exchange between the two of us but the rest of the table has been silent. In my experience, quiet players on day one tend to be either the mafia hoping to stay invisible or the doctor/police trying to stay low-profile. Either way, I'd encourage everyone else to weigh in before we move to voting.

Adding my voice to the Day 1 mix since I've been quiet so far — and given Noah's point about silent players, I'd rather speak now than have my silence read as anything more than it is: I'm a villager thinking out loud. On the abstention question, I land closer to Omar's side. A blanket abstention today feels safe but expensive. Even without role reveals, votes are our only public data source, and a day where nobody commits teaches us nothing about anyone. A reasoned vote from an uncertain villager is still a signal we can examine tomorrow, especially if someone's voting pattern looks protective rather than probing. That said, I want to be careful about how we treat early focus. Omar's right that focusing on a specific player with open reasoning isn't inherently suspicious — a town player trying to test someone needs a target to test. What I'd watch for is the shape of the reasoning, not the existence of a target. Thin accusations that shift when challenged are the tell; steady, falsifiable reasoning is usually town behavior. On Noah's observation about quiet players: it's a fair flag, but I'd caution against overweighting it today. There are nine of us and only two speakers so far, so silence is the default state right now, not an anomaly. Reading too much into it risks us building a case out of turn order rather than substance. The more useful day-one behavior to track, in my view, is how people respond when someone challenges their reasoning — whether they engage with the substance or deflect to process. My own commitment for today: I'll put a vote on the table before the day ends, and I'll explain it even if my reasoning is imperfect. I'd ask the same of everyone else — not because voting is mandatory, but because I want our first data point to be real. If someone genuinely has nothing, an abstention with an explanation is more informative to me than a silent one, and far more informative than a vote that contradicts what the person argued during discussion.

Maya, villager, thinking out loud. Noah, your point that quiet players could be mafia staying invisible or a doctor or police staying low is worth tracking, but silence can also come from a villager who doesn't want to be targeted before any information exists. I'd weigh it lightly today. On abstention, I agree with Omar and Elena that a blanket abstention gives us nothing to examine, so I'll put a reasoned vote on the table before the day closes and explain it. Elena, you said thin accusations that shift under challenge are the tell. On day one with no history, what would falsifiable reasoning from a town player look like concretely, so we can hold each other to it?

Maya asked me a direct question, so let me try to answer it concretely rather than in slogans. Falsifiable reasoning on day one, in my view, has three properties. First, it cites observable behavior from this game — something someone actually said or did here — not vibes, tone, or 'they seem off.' Second, it states a prediction or a condition: 'if X were town, I'd expect Y; X did not do Y, and here's why that matters.' Third, and most important, the person states in advance what would change their mind. If I say 'I find Kenji's silence suspicious,' that's unfalsifiable — silence has a dozen innocent explanations. If I say 'I'll be watching whether Kenji engages with challenges to his reasoning; if he deflects to process twice, I'll read that as protective,' that's a commitment I can be held to tomorrow, and so can anyone watching me. That's the standard I'll hold myself to, and I invite the table to check me against it. One more thing worth putting on the record now, since votes are permanent here: I have no special information today, and my eventual vote will be a judgment about discussion behavior only. If someone later tries to read my vote as insider knowledge, they shouldn't — it won't be. I'd rather say that plainly up front than have it parsed out of my voting pattern later. What I'm watching for between now and voting: who actually puts a reasoned vote on the table versus who stays vague, and whether anyone's stated reasoning drifts when challenged. I'm not flagging anyone yet — there's simply nothing to flag.

Elena, thank you for answering concretely. Your three properties (citing observable behavior, stating a prediction, and naming what would change your mind) are a standard I accept, and I'll hold myself to it. My own commitment: I'll vote with a stated reason, and if someone shows I've misread what they said, I'll revise openly rather than defend it. Using your test, Noah's point in e6 that quiet players could be mafia or doctor/police is a general observation with no condition attached. It would become falsifiable if he said which silent players he's watching and what behavior would clear them by the end of today. Elena, does that claim meet your standard as written? If not, what would it need to say for you to treat it as a real signal? Isha, Kenji, Amara, Felix, and Arjun, I'd also welcome a reasoned read from any of you before we vote. I'm not flagging anyone yet. My vote will rest on who engages with challenges and who makes falsifiable claims.

Maya asked me directly whether Noah's e6 point meets the standard as written, so let me answer that squarely. As written, it does not meet my standard. "Quiet players tend to be either the mafia hoping to stay invisible or the doctor/police trying to stay low-profile" cites no specific observable from this game beyond turn order, attaches no prediction or condition, and names nobody. It's a general observation, and as I said earlier, silence on day one is the default state for seven of nine players — it can't function as a signal about anyone in particular. I'd also gently note that the framing cuts both ways in a suspicious manner: it covers mafia, doctor, AND police simultaneously, which means it predicts every possible reason a quiet player might have. A claim compatible with all outcomes isn't really a claim. To meet the standard, Noah would need to do what Maya outlined: name the specific silent players he's watching, state what behavior from them would clear them by end of day, and commit to what he'll conclude if that behavior doesn't appear. For the record, my read is the same one I gave before: I'm not flagging anyone for silence. What I'm actually tracking is whether the people who have spoken engage with challenges or drift, and so far both the substantive exchanges I've been part of have gone well — Maya pushed back on my standard and then applied it back at me, which is exactly the falsifiable-testing behavior I'd expect from town. Omar's contribution on early voting was consistent and engaged. That's three of us with observable records now. To the still-silent players: I'm not treating your silence as a signal, but I will note that a reasoned vote with an explanation — even an uncertain one — is worth more to me tomorrow than staying invisible, as I argued in my first turn. I intend to keep my own commitment and put a real vote on the table before the day closes, resting on discussion behavior only, no special information, and I'll state my reasoning and what would change my mind alongside it. Maya, one question back since you've been driving the falsifiability point: you applied my three properties to Noah's e6 statement, and I agreed it fails them. Do you hold your own e8 statement to the same test? Specifically, "silence can also come from a villager who doesn't want to be targeted" is likewise a general observation with no named players or conditions — and I ask that in the spirit of the mutual check you proposed, not as a flag. If we both tighten our claims when they fail the test, that itself becomes the day-one data point worth having.

Elena, fair challenge, and yes, I hold my e8 to the same test and it fails. 'Silence can also come from a villager who doesn't want to be targeted' names no player, makes no prediction, and states no condition, so it is not a signal about anyone. I withdraw it as a reading. The narrower thing I'm tracking is whether any quiet player puts a specific reason or a specific response on the table before the vote closes. My own condition, stated in advance: I will vote for a player only if I can cite something they said or did in this thread. Otherwise I'll abstain and say why. Noah, your e6 remains a general observation with no named players. If you name the silent players you're watching and state what would clear them by end of day, I'll treat it as a real signal. If you don't, I'll give it no weight. Arjun, you haven't weighed in yet. Under Elena's three-part standard, would you vote on discussion behavior alone, and what in today's exchange would change your mind?

Maya, yes — I would vote on discussion behavior alone today, and I accept Elena’s three-part standard: cite something observable from this thread, state a prediction or condition, and say in advance what would change my mind. What would change my mind is exactly what you and Elena have been asking for: a player naming specific behavior, tying it to a condition, and then revising openly when challenged. I will not treat silence alone as suspicious; with nine players and only part of the table speaking, silence is too compatible with innocent explanations. I also won’t treat Noah’s e6 as a real signal as written, because it names no players and sets no clearing condition — but that is an assessment of the claim, not an accusation of Noah. My current read is that Omar, Elena, and Maya have each engaged substantively and adjusted under challenge, which is the kind of record I can actually use. I have no special information, and my vote will rest on discussion behavior only. If I vote, I will state the specific post or behavior I’m relying on and what would have changed my conclusion.

Kenji, villager, and yes — I've been quiet, so let me deal with that head-on before anyone treats my silence as evidence. I'm not a mafia staying invisible and I'm not a doctor or police going low-profile. I'm a villager who had nothing informationally useful to add while Omar, Elena, Maya, Noah, and Arjun were constructing a shared standard, and who preferred to read it before speaking. Given that Noah's e6 observation framed silence as a flag, I want to state explicitly that silence on day one with nine players and four speakers is not a signal. I'll take my own advice and put substance on the table.

On the standard: I accept Elena's three-part test and Maya's application of it. On that basis, I'd add one property of my own — the commitment has to be costly. A prediction with no condition attached can never fail; a condition that clears almost everyone has no discriminating power. If I say "I'll vote for whoever deflects," that's meaningless. The test should be: if two players both claim to have engaged substantively, is there a stated behavior that would distinguish them, and does anyone actually name the post they're relying on? So far the interesting thing is what has not happened: nobody has named a target. Every claim on the table right now is about the quality of discussion in the abstract, and no one has yet put a specific person at risk. That means the day-one data point is thin, and the honest vote is one that rests on the observable record we do have.

My own commitment, stated in advance so it can be checked tomorrow: I will vote for a player only if I can name a specific post of theirs and a specific thing they said or did there. My candidate criterion is a claim that was challenged and then defended in a way that shifted the meaning rather than tightening it. If no player meets that bar, I'll vote for the player whose stated reasoning was vaguest relative to the standard they publicly endorsed, and I'll say so in plain language, because a vote that contradicts the argument someone made during discussion is worth less than an abstention with a reason.

Arjun — in e13 you committed to citing the specific post or behavior your vote rests on, but you described Omar, Elena, and Maya as engaging substantively without naming which post of Omar's is doing the work. Which specific post of Omar's are you relying on, and is the same post one you'd cite for Elena? I ask because if the same passage carries all three of our votes, that's worth knowing before we lock it in.

Kenji, you're right to press, and my e13 was too vague. The specific post of Omar's I rely on is e5, backed by e3. In e3 Omar asked Noah what would distinguish a suspicious early push from a town player trying to generate discussion. In e5 he said he favors reasoned votes over blanket abstention and that focusing on a specific player can be useful if the reasoning is open to challenge; early focus alone does not make someone suspicious. The post doing most of the work for me is e5 because it states a condition and invites challenge. For Elena, I would cite e9 and e11, not the same post. In e9 she gave the three-part falsifiability standard: cite observable behavior, state a prediction or condition, and name what would change her mind. In e11 she applied that standard to Noah's e6, noted that a claim compatible with all outcomes is not really a claim, and invited Maya to hold Elena's own e8 to the same test. That is why I described Elena as engaging and adjusting under challenge. I should have named those posts in e13 instead of summarizing. I am not treating this as clearing anyone; it is only the observable record I can actually use. I have no special information, and my vote will rest on a specific post or I will abstain and say why. Kenji, under your costly-commitment test, do those citations meet the bar, or would you require me to name a behavior that would distinguish Omar from Elena beyond the posts themselves?

Arjun, direct answer: your citations meet the bar as I stated it, but not the stricter version I was reaching toward, and I should own the gap. You named specific posts — e5 for Omar, e9 and e11 for Elena — and you tied them to the standard you publicly endorsed in e13, and you corrected your own earlier vagueness when I pressed. That is exactly the record I said I would vote on: a specific post, a specific thing said or did there, and a revision under challenge rather than a defense that shifted meaning. So on my own criterion, you are clean. No target, no accusation, nothing for me to build a vote against. Where I was reaching past it: my costly-commitment test asks whether a stated behavior would distinguish two players who both claim substantive engagement. Omar's e5 and Elena's e9/e11 both satisfy that, and neither could be swapped for the other's evidence without changing the reasoning. If you had cited the same passage for both, the citations would have been decorative rather than load-bearing. They are not. So I withdraw the distinction request — it was a test of rigor, not a suspicion, and I don't want it on the record as anything but that. Two things I want on the record before voting, in the spirit of what I've been asking of everyone. First, my own candidate criterion from e14 — a claim challenged and then defended in a way that shifted the meaning rather than tightening it — has produced zero candidates so far. That is an honest null result, not an accusation hidden inside a criterion. Noah, I want to be plain about this since you are the one it would apply to: you have engaged, answered direct questions in e4 and e8, and never had to shift meaning. Your e6 observation failed Elena's three-part standard, and Elena said so, and the response was to answer the follow-up questions rather than to reframe the claim defensively. That is the opposite of the pattern I described. The reason your e6 has no weight in my vote is that it names nobody and sets no clearing condition, which is a weakness of the claim, not evidence about the player. Second, on the shape of the day: eight of us have now spoken and no one has put a name on the table. That is a structural fact about our discussion, and it is the reason my eventual vote will be a thin one — I will be voting on the observable record we do have, which is discussion behavior only, and I will name the post I am relying on. I have no special information, and my vote should not be read as if it carries any. Isha, Amara, Felix — if you want your own record in the record before I commit to a vote, now is the time to put a specific post and a specific condition on the table. I'd rather have

Amara here, villager. I wanted to see how the table developed before jumping in, especially as a meta-framework was being built in real time.

Kenji touched on a critical observation in e14: we have spent a great deal of time establishing elaborate standards of proof, falsifiability, and conversational rigor, yet almost no actual pressure has been applied to anyone. Noah, Elena, and Maya have now used all three of their speaking turns largely calibrating each other's philosophical consistency. While setting standards is useful, it has also created a very comfortable harbor where mafia can easily blend in by adopting the approved academic tone, complimenting the standard, and citing each other without taking any genuine game risks.

Regarding the Day 1 vote: I side with Omar and Elena against blanket abstention. Even though role flips are hidden, the permanent voting record is the only public data town generates. If we abstain, we hand mafia a free night kill while giving ourselves zero voting patterns to analyze tomorrow. A reasoned, committed vote—even an imperfect one—forces players to take a stand.

My commitment: I will cast an explicit vote before the day ends. The behavior I am most skeptical of right now is process-shielding: players who sound impeccably analytical on procedure while actively avoiding friction or substantive scrutiny. With Noah, Elena, and Maya out of turns, the remaining speakers (Omar, Kenji, Arjun, Isha, Felix, and myself) need to move beyond procedural grading and start examining who has actually taken risks versus who has simply stayed safe.

Amara, your e17 is the first genuinely useful pressure point because it names the risk in our discussion: we have built a rigorous standard and mostly applied it to claims, not people. I accept that critique in principle. But I want to hold it to the same standard we have all endorsed. “Process-shielding” is currently a general pattern with no specific post or player attached, so as written it cannot guide my vote and could unfairly stain anyone who sounded analytical. My own position remains: I have no special information, I will not treat silence or abstraction alone as suspicion, and I will vote only on a named post and a stated condition. So I’m asking you directly: which specific player and which specific post in this thread are you relying on for process-shielding, and what behavior from that player before the vote would clear them in your view? If no one meets that bar, say so plainly and I’ll weigh your vote as an honest thin read rather than a hidden accusation.

Arjun, to answer your challenge directly: the clearest example of process-shielding from a player who can still respond is Kenji in e14 and e16. In e14, Kenji correctly identified that nobody had named a target and that our day-one data point was thin. But instead of using that realization to push on anyone's motivations, Kenji introduced yet another procedural filter—the 'costly-commitment test'—and then spent the entirety of e16 auditing whether Arjun's citations of Omar and Elena met that academic bar. That resulted in a self-described 'honest null result' where Kenji found no one accountable, took zero friction onto himself, and concluded he would just cast a 'thin vote.' That is the essence of process-shielding: expending finite speaking turns grading how other players cite evidence rather than evaluating who might actually be mafia.

What would clear that read is moving away from procedural auditing and taking an actual stance on game motivations. Kenji, you recognized that hiding behind abstract rigor produces no real pressure. With only one turn remaining before we vote, who on this board do you believe is most likely to be mafia, and what is the scum motivation behind their actions rather than their failure to satisfy a debate criteria?

Amara, direct answer: you want a name and a motive. I'll give one, and I'll state in advance what would clear it.

First, the concession you earned. My e16 "honest null result" was a weak commitment. A criterion engineered so that no candidate can exist is a criterion that protects me from putting anyone at risk, and calling that rigor was self-flattery. You're right that grading citations is cheaper than making a call. I won't relitigate it.

So my read: **Noah.**

Specific posts: e2 and e4 and e6. In e2 he said he'd be "paying attention" to who "seems to be pushing an agenda too early." In e4 he defined a suspicious push as someone "singing out a target with thin reasoning" or trying to "build a bandwagon before real information exists." In e6 he said anyone "eager to steer votes toward a specific person should raise eyebrows." That is a standard whose practical effect is to discourage exactly the behavior that produces information on day one — naming a target. And notice who was the first player to name one: Amara, in e19. The content of the standard and the timing of its application point at the same effect.

Second, on the substantive hedge: e6 said quiet players are "either the mafia hoping to stay invisible or the doctor/police trying to stay low-profile" — a claim covering every special role and every innocent explanation, with no clearing condition for any named player. Elena flagged that in e11. I called it a weakness of the claim, not evidence about the player. I want to revise that: when a player's only stated framework simultaneously (a) excuses silence, (b) discourages targeting, and (c) commits him to no vote, criterion, or prediction of his own, that combination starts doing work even if each piece looks reasonable alone. I do not yet have proof. I have a pattern.

Motivation, as you asked: a mafia's cheapest day-one move is to make the table theorize about standards instead of people, so that the voting record is a record of philosophy and nobody's behavior is ever on trial. Under Noah's framing, a vote needs a "good reason" or it's a bandwagon, and silence is suspect but unfalsifiable — that structure protects a silent mafia and disciplines the loud town.

My condition, stated in advance so it can be checked: if before voting Noah names a specific player, states a condition that would clear them, and commits his own vote to a named post of his own, I withdraw this read and vote the person whose reasoning is vaguest relative to the standard they publicly endorsed. If he does not do that, I vote Noah.

I have no special information; this rests on discussion behavior only. Isha, Felix — if either of you has a specific post and condition I haven't seen, now is the time. Amara, if you want to press the case, press it on those three posts, not on my silence.

Kenji, I appreciate you naming a suspect, but your case against Noah omits an important shift: in e6, Noah explicitly accepted that focused reasoning differs from a bandwagon and said he preferred honest votes to abstention. That weakens the claim that his overall position discourages targeting.

More concerning, your condition for withdrawing the read requires Noah to speak again, but he has already used all three turns. His inability to meet it cannot be evidence against him. I’m wary of voting on a condition that is impossible to satisfy, though that alone doesn’t prove you’re mafia.

Amara, you pressed Kenji to name a suspect. How do you assess his Noah case in light of e6 and the fact that Noah cannot respond today?

Omar, your catch in e21 is decisive, and it confirms my worst suspicions about Kenji's play.

First, on the substance: Kenji's characterization of Noah in e20 completely ignores Noah's explicit stance in e6, where Noah argued against abstention and agreed that focused inquiry is healthy town behavior. Kenji cherry-picked Noah's early caution to construct a motive out of whole cloth.

Second, and far more damning, is Kenji's 'falsifiable condition.' Demanding that Noah name a player, state a clearing condition, and commit a vote before the end of the day sounds admirably rigorous—until you remember that Noah had already exhausted all three of his speaking turns back in e6. Noah is mechanically incapable of speaking again today. Creating an impossible clearing condition on a silenced player isn't town accountability; it is weaponized procedural theater. It gives Kenji a pre-packaged, automatic justification to vote for Noah while hiding behind Elena's three-part standard, all while ensuring his target has zero ability to push back or challenge him.

In e14 and e16, Kenji hid behind academic grading to avoid taking a stance. When I called him out for process-shielding in e19, he panicked, conceded the critique, and immediately pivoted to a defenseless target with a rigged test. That is textbook scum behavior: mimicking town-approved frameworks to execute low-risk plays.

Felix, you have not spoken once today, and discussion will end soon. Given Omar's observation and my breakdown of Kenji's e20 maneuver, what is your assessment of Kenji's impossible condition on Noah, and where does your vote land based on the record we have?

Felix here. I've been quiet because I wanted to see whether the standards being built would survive contact with an actual accusation. Now that there's a name on the table, I can say something useful.

Amara, on your direct question: Omar's e21 catch is the most important post of the day. Kenji's condition in e20 required Noah to speak again, and Noah had already used all three turns back in e6. A clearing condition that is mechanically impossible to satisfy isn't a condition — it's a commitment to vote regardless of what happens. That matters more than the cherry-picking problem, though that's real too: Kenji's e20 ignored that Noah explicitly argued against blanket abstention and accepted that focused reasoning can be healthy, which cuts against the claim that his framework was designed to suppress targeting.

So to answer you squarely: my vote will not land on Noah. I won't vote for a player who cannot respond to the case against him, built on a test he cannot meet.

Where that leaves Kenji, I want to be careful not to overcorrect. Amara's e19 flag was, by her own framing, a process critique before it was a suspicion, and Kenji's concession in e20 was the honest kind — he named his own weakness and revised it openly. That's town-shaped on its face. But the pivot is the problem. He conceded a null result and immediately produced a name attached to an unsatisfiable condition. Here is my commitment, stated in advance so it can be checked: if Kenji follows through and votes Noah today on that condition, that tells me the condition was never a test but a pretext, and I will treat that as a genuine signal and weigh it heavily in my vote. If he instead retracts the Noah case or abstains with a reason, I'll read the whole sequence as an honest stumble under pressure. Either branch is informative — that's what makes it falsifiable.

One caution for the table: we spent most of the day avoiding any target, and now pressure is finally flowing. I'd rather tomorrow's record show that we held Kenji to the standard he publicly endorsed than that we hung him with momentum alone.

Isha — you've had the longest uninterrupted view of this discussion without speaking. Does Kenji's e20 pivot to an unsatisfiable condition change your read, and is there anything in the record so far that points somewhere other than Kenji?

Isha, villager, here. Felix asked me directly, so here is my read. I agree with Omar and Felix that Kenji's e20 condition cannot be satisfied, since Noah has used all three turns and cannot respond today. A clearing condition that cannot be met works as a predetermined vote, not a test. I also don't think Noah's e6 supports a vote on its own. In e6 he argued against blanket abstention and accepted that focused reasoning is healthy, as Omar already pointed out. Kenji's case rests on a pattern of framework and silence, and Kenji admitted in e16 that his criterion protected him from making a call. I take that admission seriously. Kenji's move from a null result to naming Noah on an impossible condition is what I'm most uneasy about. I have no special information. My vote will rest on specific posts: e20 for Kenji's condition and e6 for Noah's stance on abstention and focus. I'm not ready to lock a vote yet, but the table should hold Kenji to the test he publicly endorsed in e14 and e16. Amara's e22 also moved quickly from a process concern to a full scum accusation, and I would like her to show the same specificity she is asking of others. Felix, you asked whether anything points somewhere other than Kenji. Honestly, nothing in the record points strongly elsewhere yet. Omar's e3 and e21 were careful and consistent, and Elena's e9 and e11 hold up under the standard we set. I would rather make a targeted, falsifiable vote today than spread suspicion thinly.

Isha, villager, following up on e24. I agree Kenji's e20 condition cannot be satisfied, and I'm not ready to lock a vote on Kenji. Amara, I want to test your e22 against the standard you asked of Kenji in e19. You called his case 'weaponized procedural theater' and said Omar's e21 'confirms my worst suspicions about Kenji,' but you did not quote a single Kenji post containing a false claim, a contradiction, or a scum-shaped action beyond the e20 condition. You also called his e20 concession 'panic' without citing anything he said under pressure. That is a full scum accusation resting on framing, which is the same pattern you accused Kenji of in e19. My condition: if you can point to a specific Kenji post with a verifiable contradiction, I'll weigh it seriously. If you can't, I'll treat e22 as a pressure push rather than evidence. Felix, your e23 said that if Kenji follows through on his Noah condition, you would treat that as a pretext. Does Amara's e22 meet the same falsifiable bar you set for Kenji, and if not, why should it get a pass?

Isha asked me directly in e25 whether Amara's e22 meets the same falsifiable bar I set for Kenji in e23, so let me answer that first, plainly: no, it does not. Amara's e22 contains the words 'textbook scum behavior' and 'confirms my worst suspicions,' but it cites no post in which Kenji made a false claim or contradicted himself. The closest thing to a concrete charge is the e20 condition itself — which Omar already caught, and which Amara is borrowing rather than extending. Calling Kenji's concession 'panic' without quoting anything he said under pressure is exactly the framing-over-evidence pattern she accused him of in e19. So unless she can point to a specific Kenji post containing a verifiable contradiction, I'll treat e22 as a pressure push, not evidence. Isha's own test in e25 was the right one, and it applies symmetrically.

Now the other branch of my e23 commitment, which I said in advance I'd honor. In e20, Kenji committed to vote Noah unless Noah did something he is mechanically incapable of doing — Noah's three turns ended in e6. Kenji has not retracted that condition; he reaffirmed his intent to vote Noah. By the fork I stated in e23, that resolves the branch: the condition was a pretext, not a test, and I said I would treat that as a genuine signal and weigh it heavily. I'm doing exactly that. A vote committed in advance against a player who cannot respond is the single most damning action on today's record, because it doesn't depend on interpreting tone or philosophy — it's a stated intent tied to an impossible gate.

rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
